en: The Method for the Recitation of the Tāre-Heart Mantra of the Lotus Family,
compiled by the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi of South India.
This essential manual on the gate of recitation is intended primarily for the accomplishment of the Tāre-Heart Bodhisattva, yet it is also applicable to all other families.
When practicing, one must consult with those who are learned in the Dharma to resolve doubts and finalize the clear mantras, mudrās, and all other sequential procedures;

do not add or subtract anything further. This dharma-gate is joined with and integrated into the various sūtra-dharma gates and yoga-gates so that beginners seeking liberation may attain the stages and levels; thus, it is compiled and perfected for the cultivation of those practices.
Regarding this gateway, one should first enter the Great Samaya Maṇḍala, receive the bodhisattva precepts, and practice the bodhisattva conduct.

Arousing a mind of great compassion, one should benefit sentient beings by relinquishing body, life, and wealth. With a mind single-mindedly aspiring toward the Buddha’s bodhi-body, one should remain unattached to greed or anger, exerting oneself with vigor, and maintaining a concentrated mind free from distraction.
One’s mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity should never cease for even a moment.

Constantly make the vow to cause all boundless sentient beings to cross over to the other shore. One who practices this Dharma should purify themselves internally and externally, making them utterly pure and pristine.
Toward elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), and instructors (*ācārya*), one should always show respect with a mind free from flattery or crookedness;
one's speech should be truthful, and one must not violate their instructions of trust. One should practice giving according to one’s means and must not harbor greedy attachment.
In the practice of giving material wealth, let there be no interval between the four postures; do not allow it to be interrupted, but constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Do not dwell on thoughts of form or desire, nor indulge in negligence or self-indulgence, nor engage in various worldly affairs.

In the intervals between these, at every single moment and instant, clarify your mindfulness and observe with discernment that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent. To speak briefly, all dharmas are like a mirror.
Once you have understood this, you must don the armor of diligence, destroy the army of afflictions with the sword of secret mantra, and completely shatter the web of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Emerging from the delusory ocean of birth and death, proceed to the site of enlightenment and sit upon the Vajra Seat;
resolve your own mind so that it never regresses. Only those who direct their attention in this way should cultivate this Mahāyāna treasury of precepts.
This is the most supreme dharma-gate; therefore, I shall explain it in sequence. One who wishes to perform recitation should first purify the ground.

Regarding the measurement for the purification of the site, one should measure out the ground—whether four cubits, eight cubits, eleven cubits, sixteen cubits, or other such measures—and from among these measurements, take as much as one’s strength allows.
One should dig to a depth of reaching the knee or one cubit, and clear away insects, ants, and the like.

Having filled the pure land with all manner of impure and foul objects such as tiles, rubble, hair, bones, ashes, charcoal, chaff, husks, thorns, roots, and stalks, and having made it firm and level, one should then construct a sublime vihāra upon it and thoroughly smear its interior with pure plaster.
First, one must determine the cardinal directions; if one seeks the rite for the removal of calamities, the vihāra should have its southern gate opened.
When sitting facing north, one should sit with the two calves crossed.
If performing rites for increase (*puṣṭi*), one should open the western gate, face east, and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

If performing wrathful rites (*krodha*), one should open the northern gate, face south, and sit in a squatting position with the left foot pressing upon the right. If performing rites for friendship and intimacy, [one should sit]...
One should open the eastern gate and sit facing west with both legs extended and the two knees apart; this is called the posture for constructing a vihāra and seeking success.
The method for the mantra-reciter’s sitting, rising, forming mudrās, and performing the ritual has been briefly explained.
Whether there is already a purified chamber, or on an open space, or upon mountain rocks and the like, it is sufficient to construct the maṇḍala according to the circumstances.
If one seeks to accomplish any matter, performing it according to the ritual in its entirety, all wishes will be fulfilled.

First, regarding a room that has already been plastered and decorated, one should take [the materials] and recite the mantra over them; only then should they be used. If one wishes to purify the ground again, one should sweep it until it is clean.
When first sweeping the ground, one should recite this mantra, which says:
Oṃ hara hara rauru gṛhṇa haraṇaya svāhā.
Having recited this three times and swept away [the obstacles], when removing what was above, one should again recite the subsequent mantra, saying:

Oṃ (1) stute mahāstute (2) śuddhane svāhā. Having finished reciting the mantra, one should remove the [impurities] from that place and smear the altar with cow dung; at that time, the mantra is as follows:

Oṃ (1) karale (2) mahākarale (2) svāhā. Recite this mantra for the purpose of anointing the ground of the altar, washing the offering vessels, and consecrating the vessels for fragrant water. The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) karale (2) mahākarale (2) svāhā.
Recite this mantra for the purpose of anointing the ground of the altar, washing the offering vessels, and consecrating the vessels for fragrant water. The mantra is as follows:
Namo siddhirnāthāya sarvatathāgatebhyaḥ | Oṃ vīre vīre mahāvajri sata sata sarate sarate taraye taraye vidamani svadhāni ||
(8) Taramati (10) Siddha (9) Gṛhīte jvāle (11) Svāhā. Having recited this mantra three times, one washes all the ritual implements.
The reason for reciting this mantra is to purify and remove all faults of defilement resulting from violations of the *samaya* vows.
This applies to food vessels as well as offerings of incense and flowers.
Before the items to be offered have been fully presented, gather them all together and place them in one pure location.
Recite this vidyā-mantra and form mudrās for protection. The mantra is: Oṃ (1) śikhari (2) vajri (3) ti (4).
To form the mudrā, clench the three fingers from the middle finger downward of the right hand around the thumb to make a fist, and extend the index finger straight upward.
With this seal, stamp it upon the objects; rotate it to the right to serve as a protection for all incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, food, drink, and so forth.
Once these preparations are complete, the practitioner shall then proceed to the bathing place to perform the rite.
Regarding these rites, whether performed by oneself or caused to be performed by a disciple, one gains the same merit.
When wishing to bind the mudrās, one should first bind the three Samaya-mudrās; only after that may one bind the various other mudrās.
As for the characteristics of the Samayas: first, the Buddha Samaya-mudrā is formed by placing both hands side-by-side with palms touching, as if normally holding an object.
Place the tip of the index finger upon the upper part of the middle finger, and then place the tip of the thumb upon the lower part of the index finger;
this constitutes the mudrā. The mantra is: Oṃ (1) Tathāgata (2) Nābhāya (3) Svāhā.
While reciting this mantra, raise the mudrā and place it upon the crown of the head, forming the mental visualization that this mudrā is itself the body of the Buddha.
Next, the Lotus Samaya Mudrā is explained:
join the wrists of both hands, extend the ten fingers of both hands, and place the two thumbs side by side.
Placing the two little fingers likewise, one forms the seal and raises it to rest upon the crown of the head, as if near the right side;
while doing so, one should form this thought: "This seal is the Noble Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Then he spoke the mantra:
Oṃ (1) Padma-nābhaya (2) Svāhā (3). Next, the Vajrasamaya-mudrā is explained: with both hands, the right presses down upon the left;
that is, the right little finger is interlaced with the left thumb, and the right thumb [is interlaced] with the left [thumb].
Interlace the fingers with the left little finger to form the mudrā and recite the mantra: Oṃ (1) vajra-nābha-ya (2) svāhā (3).
Having raised the mudrā and placed it upon the crown of the head near the left side, visualize yourself as Vajra; this is the triple samaya.
Once the seal has been formed, one may then bind all other seals. One should follow the secret treasury of the Mantra Kings of the three families and practice according to this method.

To further explain its essentials: when a practitioner first rises in the early morning and is about to go out before having performed any other activity, they should perform this rite; thus, whenever entering or exiting, they should first form the seal.
Having first performed the visualization and recited the vidyā-mantra, one may then proceed with the practice. The vidyā-mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ ratnatrayāya (1) Namo śrīcaṇḍavajrapāṇaye (2) Mahāyakṣasenāpataye (3) Namo vajrakrodhāya (4)
Jaye (4) danturakaṭa-piśāca-āye (5) tadyathā (6) oṃ (7) amṛta-kumārī (8) kha kha (9) khāhi khāhi (10) tiṣṭha tiṣṭha (11) bandha bandha (12) hana hana (13) gaja gaja (14) viśva... (14) (Note:
The provided text fragment appears to be a portion of a dhāraṇī or mantra. The final term "viśva" is cut off.)
Bhūṭaye viśvabhūṭaye (15) sarvaviṣanāgavighnamahāgaṇapate (16) eṣa tvam atikarṇa (17) hūṃ phaṭ (18) svāhā.
Recite this mantra while using both hands to pinch the nails of the little fingers with the thumbs, extending the remaining three fingers.
Then cross both arms, placing the right over the left, each resting upon the shoulder; this constitutes the heart-mudrā. One should then form the visualization:
stand with the feet in the shape of the character "八" (eight), puff out the cheeks, bite the right lip, and assume an expression of wrath while reciting the mantra seven times.
This is called "Averting Demons. If one wishes to bind obstructing spirits and ghosts, one should then raise both hands three times.
Pointing [with the finger] binds all obstacles; when binding all obstacles, one should say "Paṇḍa paṇḍa. Having performed this rite, one should then leave the room.
If one performs the recitation rite, at the time of bathing, one should take pure earth, burn it with fire until it is well-cooked, and grind it into a fine powder.
Once powdered, place it in a vessel; then, having formed the mudrā and recited the mantra, proceed further.
If it has not been purified, do not employ this mudrā. To form it: with both hands, interlace the three fingers from the index downward, right over left, facing outward;
join them together and extend the two index fingers straight up, with the two thumbs standing upright beside them.
The mantra is as follows: [Mantra]
Oṃ (1) nikhaṇa (2) vāsude (3) svāhā. Having recited this mantra three times, one should touch the ground with the mudrā;

only then is it called "purified" and may it be used. When a practitioner of the Dharma goes to various places, they should first protect their body with this mudrā. This mudrā is formed with the two little fingers of both hands...
Place the ring fingers together with the right pressing over the left, interlacing them toward the inside; hold the two middle fingers straight upright with their tips touching;

place the two index fingers alongside the middle fingers so that the upper joints touch the back of the hands at a distance of one *fen*; keep the two thumbs upright and press the middle joints of the fingers together.
Then recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ (1) Vajra-jñī-pratipātaya (3) Svāhā. Using this mudrā, one should seal five places:
the head, the two shoulders, the heart, and the throat; these are called the five places, and only after sealing them may one proceed.
This is the method for protecting the body. When going to the latrine, one should first snap the fingers three times to alert [any spirits].
Afterward, he performed the *añjali-mudrā* (finger-snap) and recited the mantra: *Oṃ kili kili kīla-laki kīla hūṃ phaṭ*.
One should snap the fingers once for each recitation up to three times before entering the latrine; likewise when performing the purification.
While maintaining mindfulness of the preceding Mañjuśrī mantra and its form, one should then wash the hands. Once the hand-washing is complete, one should rinse the mouth.
Having finished rinsing the mouth, one should seal the mouth with the mudrā:

bend the middle and ring fingers of the right hand into the palm, and extend the thumb, index, and little fingers straight upward to receive the water. Use this to rinse the mouth three times, reciting the mantra as follows:
Oṃ (1) sthu sthu li (2) kuru kuru (3) svāhā.
Having rinsed the mouth with this seal-mantra, one should again perform the seal-mantra for purifying and removing the invisible obstructing spirits and deities within the body:
form fists with both hands, extend the two index fingers, and grasp the right index finger within the left fist.
At the left head [of the image], point with the index finger;
do the same for the right. The mantra is: Oṃ (1) hana hana (2) amṛte (3) hūṃ phaṭ.
Recite the mantra three times and, using the mudrā, slowly stroke from the head downward three times. This will enable one to...
Visualize that all demonic obstacles within the body are completely extinguished.
Once you know that the various demons have departed, again perform the Binding of All Demons Seal; this seal is the Great Wrathful Vajra Seal.
One should support it outwardly with the left hand, then turn the back of the right hand over onto the back of the left hand, interlacing the eight fingers, and then [turn] the left...
Rotate [the hands] so they face the heart, forming fists; then extend both thumbs and place them upon the heart.
Next, tuck the right elbow inside the left elbow, draw it outward, and with the seal placed upon the head, release the seal and lower it slowly. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) kili kili (2) vimarodara (3) prakṛti (4) mahā-kuruta (5) viśaya (6) nikrandata (7) hūṃ hūṃ (8) phaṭ (9) paṇḍa paṇḍa svāhā (10).
By the power of this seal-mantra, one is able to bind all Māras and their like;
furthermore, by visualizing oneself clad in adamantine armor, one causes the palace of Māra to tremble and become restless, so that they all come to surrender.
Again, divide the pure land into three parts; while dividing the ground, once more perform the seal-mantra, using the thumb of the right hand to press the little finger.
Having placed this mudrā at the right side of the waist, one should likewise form this same mudrā with the left hand and sprinkle water upon the earth,
reciting the mantra: Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ.
Recite this mantra three times and sprinkle [the earth] with it; thereafter, use soil. Furthermore, perform the rite for purifying water:
bend the left thumb into the palm, then bend the middle and ring fingers to press down upon the thumb;
next, hook the index and little fingers, placing the tips of these two fingers against the middle joints of the middle and ring fingers.
Turning one's back [to the object], with the right hand, press the tip of the little finger with the thumb and extend the remaining three fingers straight;
cross the hands over the waist and bend the left arm so that the hand points outward. The mantra is as follows:
*Namo vajra hūṃ* (1) *hana dhuna* (2) *matha viśvaṃ saṃyojaya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Recite this mantra seven times while forming the aforementioned mudrā and enter into the water— whether it be a river, the ocean, or a pond.
Form this seal for all [rituals]. When using mantras to store water, simply touch it with this seal before bathing.
Once you have entered the water, raise your right hand and do not let go; wave it below, in the four directions, and above to establish a boundary (*sīmābandha*).
While waving the seal, you should recite this mantra. The mantra says: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ (1) Śaṅkari (2) Samaye (3) Svāhā. Recite this mantra three times and use it to strike and bind the boundary;

thus the boundary is established. Furthermore, when using purified earth, one should press the tip of the little finger with the thumb of the right hand while extending the other three fingers straight, and sprinkle water.
When using it upon the ground, cleansing powder (*śamīdhāvana*), and so forth, the mantra is: Oṃ (1) kili kili (2) vajra (3) hūṃ phaṭ.
Furthermore, to purify water for rinsing, one should interlace the three fingers below the index fingers of both hands with the palms facing inward.
Bend the tips of the two index fingers so they touch each other, making them slightly rounded rather than square;
hold the two thumbs side by side upright and recite the mantra: *Oṃ hana vajra vajriṇa ha*.
Reciting this mantra three times, insert it into the water and stir it; this will cause all the fish and dragons within the water [to be subdued].
Furthermore, various venomous insects and other obstructing spirits will be unable to cause harm.
Moreover, when using soap powder (*kaṣāya*) or similar substances to rub and massage the body, one should bend the middle and ring fingers of the right hand and insert them both into the palm;
then, with the thumb, press down upon the tips of the nails of those two fingers, while the index and little fingers remain extended.
Directly apply the soap powder, ash, earth, or other substances used for cleansing into the palms;
first rub them on the head, and when washing the upper parts of the body, recite the mantra: Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ.
Next, when washing the lower part of the body, the mantra is: Oṃ (1) Bu (2) Śvara (3) Hūṃ.
Then, having finished washing the lower part of the body, one should again use the aforementioned mantra and mudrā for rinsing the mouth; only after rinsing should one touch the head.
When one has finished bathing and washing hands and rinsing the mouth, etc., it is done in the same manner.
Having bathed in this way, one should then cover the body with the Mañjuśrī-kavaca (Mañjuśrī Armor). For this rite, one should bend the middle and ring fingers of both hands into the palms;
then, using the thumbs of each hand, press down upon the nails of those two [fingers]. With the middle and ring fingers of both hands...
Join the middle phalanges of the ring fingers together, and touch the tips of the two index fingers and the two little fingers; the mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ ratnatrayāya (1) Namo vajracandāya (2) Vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye (3) Namo vajrakīlāya (4)
Dāna (5) praśvartita-nipāta (6) ḍiṇḍimaru-utkaṭa-paira-bhāya (7) asimu-bhara (8) vajra-praśūpa-sahabhāte (9) tadyathā (10) oṃ (11) amṛta-kumārī (12) kha kha.
Khakha (13) khana khana khana khana (14) khada khada khada khada (15) khahi khahi khahi khahi (16) tiṣṭha tiṣṭha (17) dhaha dhaha (18) pacca pacca (19) ulūhana ulūhana ulūhana (20)
Bandha bandha (21) gaja gaja (22) viṣṇubhūte viṣṇubhūte (23) bhagavan amṛta-kumāra-jambhale (24) mūla-dāna-dantake (25) vajrin sarva-vighna-vināyaka-nivāraya!
RA (26) MAHĀGAṆAPATI (27) BISAṂTAKARA (28) HŪṂ HŪṂ (29) PHAṬ PHAṬ. Recite this mantra seven times and bind it by circling the seal around the body;
imagine that the body is clad in armor, and then use this mantra once more.
Regarding the *abhiṣeka-mudrā* for consecrating with enchanted water: interlace the two little fingers with the right over the left;

then join the two ring fingers together and bend them inward; touch the tips of the two middle fingers together; place each of the two index fingers upon the upper joint of its respective middle finger;
and place each of the two thumbs against the side of its respective index finger. This constitutes the mudrā; using it, scoop up water.
To perform the consecration, recite the mantra: Oṃ (1) kha-kha-ri-ri (2) hūṃ (3) phaṭ.
Having recited this mantra three times and performed the consecration, wipe the body dry; then, once again, bind the hair on the crown of the head into a single topknot.
To bind the topknot seal: form a fist with the right hand and extend the thumb straight upward;
this is the binding of the topknot. Thereafter, perform the seal and recite the mantra: Oṃ śikhāyai svāhā.
Furthermore, when bathing, one should not bathe near mud, thorns, dangerous places, swirling eddies, rapid currents, or areas that are extremely deep or extremely shallow.

When voiding excrement, urinating, or spitting phlegm, one must never discard such impurities into springs, ponds, rivers, or wells; the same applies to the banks of rivers, ponds, springs, and wells. Or...

At times he leaps and bounds, at times he swallows and sinks, at times he floats and plays, at times he lies down, at times he turns over, and at times he gazes at his own form, giving rise to lustful thoughts.
All of these are improper; one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, not allowing the mind to become distracted.
One should regard the deity of the root mantra as no different from oneself, and regard the spirit of the root mantra, the Triple Gem, and so forth, as if they were right before one's eyes.

First, take three handfuls of the water used for bathing and offer them while forming this mudrā: with both hands, form the usual hollowed cup, but simply join the two thumbs and the two index fingers together.
First offer these to the Three Jewels, and then to one’s own tutelary deity. The mantra for offering the water is as follows:
Oṃ tiri tiri buddhāya svāhā. Oṃ tiri tiri dharmāya svāhā. Oṃ tiri tiri saṃghāya svāhā.
The root mantra for the Water Deity is as follows:
Oṃ (1) tārī (2) tud-tāri (3) tūri (4) arghaṇe (5) bhagavati (6) pratijñehaṃ (7) svāhā.
Having thus sprinkled water upon the robes according to one's capacity, one should recite the original mantra while in the water.
Then, slowly emerging from the water, one takes up the robes; while putting them on, one sprinkles water upon the garments before donning them.
Next, one takes water with both hands, forming fists to sprinkle it—this is the mudrā. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) sarvatathāgata (2) dhiṣṭhita (3) amoghapāśa (4) svāhā. Next is the mantra for the robe-binding mudrā;
as for the mudrā, it is simply to form fists with both hands. The mantra is as follows:

Oṃ (1) vaimala-pari (2) vṛta (3) vajri (4) hūṃ. Reciting this mantra, one should don the robes as well as necklaces, crowns, bracelets, rings, and all other articles for adorning the body; these are all used in conjunction with the aforementioned mantra.
While bathing, dressing, or performing the rite of protection (*rakṣā*), one must not give rise to anger in the interim.
One should not look upon any impure, foul, or inauspicious objects with wrong mindfulness.
When one has finished bathing and proceeds toward the *caitya*, one must not go barefoot;

rather, one should form the mental visualization that an eight-petaled lotus supports one's feet, and that one's own body is identical in form to that of the deity, with all [attributes] complete on both the left and right sides.
Surrounded and attended by the eight classes of nāgas and divine kings, one should visualize one’s own deity standing solemnly before oneself.
When any person who maintains this recitation wishes to go out among all those within the three realms,
whether on a distant or near journey, they must not ride upon living grass, various animals, or any items used for offerings.
One must not step over the shadows of stupas, sacred images, or the reflections of one's preceptors, parents, and others;
rather, having washed and rinsed one's mouth once more before reaching the precincts of the vihāra, one should enter. Upon first opening the door, one should enter while uttering the sound "HŪṂ.
Having entered, one should perform prostrations, maintaining this mental resolve during the prostration: "To all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three times, the Kings of all Dharmas."

It is eternally abiding and unchanging, yet ordinary beings do not perceive it with their physical eyes. Having formed this thought, one should eliminate the three delusions and cultivate the three merits.
Prostrating oneself fully on the ground with deep reverence, one should perform the salutation; at the time of prostration, with mind and speech in accord, one should speak these words:
"I now take refuge in all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Having spoken these words, one performs the salutation.

Having done so, one should kneel with both knees on the ground and, joining the palms with a sincere heart, repent of all transgressions—whether committed by oneself, taught to others, or rejoiced in upon seeing or hearing them—and thus repent of all such evils.

Having completed the repentance, one should further rejoice in all merits, make extensive great vows, and pledge to cultivate all forms of goodness and refrain from harming any living being. Having performed this rite:
Even if one places the right knee on the ground and recites this mantra while maintaining the aforementioned Vajrasamādhi-mudrā, the mantra being: Oṃ (1) Vajramite (2) Svāhā.
When forming this mudrā, by simultaneously making offerings to all Buddhas with the three karmas, it enables the practitioner to swiftly attain the vajra.
Having completed this rite with a firm body, one should sit in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) and open both eyes.
Visualize the syllable *ma* above the right eye; this syllable *ma* completely becomes a radiant sun. Visualize the syllable *ṭha* above the left eye;
this syllable *ṭha* completely becomes a bright moon. Having formed this visualization, look around in all directions like a lion.
From within his eyes, the King emits the blazing, surging, and fiercely flaming radiance of vajra-power, which scatters and burns all vināyakas;
performing this rite causes all mantra-deities to rejoice. While forming this visualization, the mantra is recited as follows:
Oṃ vajra-dhūpe ṭha. Again, burn incense, and with the smoke of this incense, drive away all demons throughout the realm of empty space above. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) pātumini (2) mū-aye mahāye (3) jayini mahāni (4) svāhā. Having recited this mantra and burned incense to purify and eliminate the māras of the upper realm of empty space,
one should then recite the *kulacittamantra* (Heart Mantra of the Family).
Mix powdered incense with water to form the boundary for the four directions, reciting the mantra:
Oṃ (1) Aruli (2) Svāhā. Having performed this rite, perform this visualization: from the syllable Hṛīḥ, Amitāyus Tathāgata emerges from this syllable.
Rising up, they flow forth as a wondrous stream of milk, thereby forming a great ocean. Within this ocean, one should visualize the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ).
This syllable *praṇava* transforms into a tortoise, its form immeasurable in length and breadth, and its color like that of gold.
Upon its back, one should visualize the syllable *hṛīḥ*. This syllable, in turn, transforms into a lotus flower; the flower is red in color. All [of these]...
There are eight petals, each with three layers. Within this flower, visualize the syllable *su*;
on both sides of the *su*, visualize a *hūṃ* syllable. This transforms into Mount Sumeru, which has eight peaks composed of various jewels.
Within this mountain, again contemplate five chambers: the central chamber arises from the syllable *hu*, and the eastern chamber arises from *hūṃ*.
The southern chamber arises from the syllable *Ta*, the western chamber from the syllable *Tra*, the northern chamber from the syllable *Hrīḥ*, and [the central chamber] from the syllable *A*.
Thus, while these five chambers appear to be distinct externally, they are in fact a single interior space.
Within this hall are eight great vajra-pillars, fashioned from exquisite jewels and interspersed with various rare and brilliant ornaments; above them are the heads of makaras.

The ivory tips of the pillars were set with precious *maṅgura* gems, from which golden bells hung; they were draped all around with *vastra-hāra* necklaces and adorned with jeweled canopies and *bodhi-flower* ornaments.
Nets of fine threads and clusters of blossoms were interlaced, their pure radiance reflecting one another.

A ground of *vaiḍūrya* and other jewels served as its base, upon which exquisite flowers such as the *kusuma* were strewn. Pure-precept sandalwood incense, uniquely fragrant and sublime, was being burned.
The fragrance of liberation wafted in dense clouds, while the brilliant, shimmering light of the *maṇi* lamp of transcendent wisdom blazed forth.

Rows of jewel trees stood in formation, and as a subtle fragrant breeze gently touched them, wondrous sounds issued forth together. Variegated banners fluttered in profusion, reflecting and obscuring one another.

Surrounded in front and behind by immeasurable varieties of yakṣas, rākṣasas, devas, and other beings, they played various musical instruments and performed the vajra dance, offering praise to the Golden One.

Just as auspicious clouds spread and rain down exquisite fragrant flowers that fill the void and fall in profusion and slow descent, various foods and drinks are arranged as offerings for those who practice the Dharma.
One should always contemplate this with a mind of profound stillness, entering into meditative observation in accordance with the mind.
When entering this contemplation, first recite this mantra, which says:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām (1). Sarvathā khaṃ (2). Udana-akṣite (3). Sipharahime (4). Gaganagañje svāhā (5). By reciting this vidyā-mantra, one enters all samādhis;
whatever is contemplated according to the mind’s intent is entirely accomplished—this is the truthful word of the Buddha.

One should not harbor doubts. The reason for first performing this contemplation is to cause both the internal and external to be pure like space, unattached to anything, and naturally pure as the pure body;
therefore, one recites this mantra together with the heart-seal (cittamudrā).
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) svabhāva-śuddhāḥ (2) sarva-dharmāḥ (3) svabhāva-śuddho ’ham. Having recited this vidyā-mantra and purified the body, he further spoke these words:
"For immeasurable kalpas, I have wandered through birth and death, submerged in the mire of afflictions;
having failed to meet a virtuous friend, I followed my own mind and was unable to emerge from the unsurpassed path."
Because one does not give rise to longing, one should now resolve upon Bodhicitta and vocally recite the syllable *A*. This syllable signifies non-arising;
it is the gateway to the gate of empty stillness. Only this gateway can distance one from dust and defilement;

those who accord with this Dharma can eliminate the sins of a traveler numbering as many as motes of dust accumulated over immeasurable kalpas. It is like the bright sun shining clearly upon a pure sky.
All darkness naturally opens up at the rising sun; here, "sun" refers to the sun of wisdom (*prajñā*) and "empty space" refers to the space of mantra.

By means of this sun of wisdom shining upon the space of mantra, the darkness of afflictions is removed. With a clear and pure mind, one contemplates the realm of empty space and beholds Tathāgatas as numerous as sesame seeds, their marks and signs fully perfected.
All these Tathāgatas appear before one, snapping their fingers to startle and awaken them, and declare:
"Good son, if you wish to resolve upon Bodhicitta, you should observe your own mind.

At that time, having received these words, the practitioner should leap for joy, rise from his seat, and go before the Buddhas. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he should pay homage with single-minded devotion.
While prostrating to the Buddhas, he should recite this mantra:
Oṃ (1) sarvatathāgata (2) pādavandanāṃ (3) karomi. Having recited this mantra and visualized paying homage to all the Tathāgatas, one should then contemplate one’s own mind.
While contemplating one’s own mind, one should recite this mantra, which says: [The mantra is as follows: Oṃ sarvatathāgata pādavandanāṃ karomi.
Oṃ (1) *citta-prativedha* (2) *karoṣi*. While reciting this vidyā-mantra, one should visualize a moon-disc within one's own heart. If it does not appear clearly, one should say to the Buddha:
"The visualization I have practiced has not yet become clear. The Buddha said: "Good son, you should recite this mantra once more."
Contemplate the mind until it is utterly clear and pure. The mantra is:

Oṃ bodhicittam utpādayāmi. Having recited this mantra and contemplated the moon of the mind until it is utterly clear and pure, one attains firm resolve for awakening (bodhicitta). Then, contemplate upon that moon.
Regarding the visualization of the single vajra-lotus: when visualizing the flower, one should recite this mantra.
The mantra is: Oṃ (1) tiṣṭha (2) vajra (3) padma. By reciting this mantra while visualizing the flower, there is a vajra upon that flower; it is named as such because of this characteristic.
It is said: "One should form this mind regarding the Vajra-lotus: 'This body of mine is neither identical to nor different from the Vajra-lotus.
Gradually it shall blossom, its radiance blazing intensely, surpassing immeasurable realms.
Upon entering this Samādhi of the Blossoming Radiance of the Vajra-lotus, one should again recite this mantra. The mantra is as follows:"
Oṃ (1) siddhara (2) vajra (3) padma. Reciting this mantra and contemplating this opening flower, its radiance illuminated immeasurable Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Within that light, the Bodhisattva Multitude of Benefits (Bahuratna) uttered a clear and resonant blue voice, speaking thus: [as requested].

When the Tathāgatas of these various lands enter into this flower, and once all these Tathāgatas have entered it, they then gradually contract this wondrous flower until it is no different from before;
according to their power, they are able to observe the size of this body and cause it to abide therein.
At the time of performing this *saṃkucita-puṣpa-samādhi*, one should recite this mantra, which says: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ (1) saṃhara (2) vajra (3) padma. Reciting this mantra, one gathers the flowers;
according to their size, having remained [in that state], one again enters the samādhi of the body of the Vajrapadma.
Fully utilizing this lotus to form one’s own body, when entering this visualization, one recites this mantra again, which says:
Oṃ vajrapadma-hūṃ-kāra-samaya hūṃ mahāsamaya hūṃ. Having thus visualized this body as the Vajra-Lotus,
one should then visualize this very body as the Noble Avalokiteśvara.
Regarding the mastery of his physical form: he sits upon a precious lotus flower and wears a precious flower crown.
Within that crown, there is the Tathāgata Amitāyus, seated upon a precious lotus flower in the mudrā of preaching the Dharma; this is called the appearance of the Tathāgata within the crown.
His left hand holds a vajra-lotus; having first formed the lotus-fist with the hand holding the flower, he then...
Extend the middle fingers and the tips of the index fingers, joining them with the thumbs; the ring fingers and little fingers are held like fists.
With this seal, hold a *vajra-flower* in the right hand as well, but pinch one petal of the flower to form the gesture of "turning the flower.
For those who contemplate in this manner, the Bodhisattvas of Great Benefit and the Noble Ones will arrive at their place of contemplation; therefore, this is performed first.

Entering this contemplation is for the purpose of establishing this body so that one may swiftly attain a firm adamantine body, and furthermore, so that in every birth one may obtain a body equal to that of a noble being without distinction. To establish this body, one should employ this seal-mantra:
with the two hands, interlace the three fingers from the index finger downward with the palms facing outward, and touch the tips of the two index fingers together as shown.
Extending both hands like lotus petals and holding up the two thumbs, recite the mantra: Oṃ kṛtsna-kārya-ādhiṣṭhāna svāhā hṛīḥ.
With this seal-mantra, one should seal the four places; the four places are the heart, the space between the eyebrows, the throat, and the crown of the head—these are the four places.
Next, perform the rite of self-consecration, which can cause the practitioner to swiftly attain the three bodies in their entirety.
To form this seal, one should join the two hands in the usual manner of *añjali* and then contract the index fingers.
With the four fingers already joined at their tips, bend the backs of those fingers to form the shape of precious lotus petals.
The mantra is: Oṃ (1) dharimaṇi-padma (2) abhiṣecana-hrīḥ. Reciting this mantra, raise the mudrā and place it against the forehead;
then release the fingers and move them around the head until they reach the back of the crown.
Gradually tracing [the breath] through the body up to the heart, one should abide in the heart. Then, forming two vajra-fists with both hands, extend the index fingers straight;
visualize the syllable *Oṃ* on the face of the right index finger and the syllable *Dhaṃ* on the face of the left index finger.
Then, intertwining the two fingers, release light from above the syllables on those fingers, which is exceedingly brilliant.
Possessing majestic power, he again encircled his body with both hands toward the back, reaching as far as his back;

likewise, he again circled from his back to above his navel, doing the same there; again, he circled from above the navel to behind his waist, and again from behind the waist, he circled completely around his seat.
Again, he moved upward from below to the front of his throat, doing the same there; then again from the throat...
From the front it reaches the crown; from the back it is likewise. From the crown it ascends to the forehead; from there it is likewise.
From this forehead it encircles to the rear of the crown. Having encircled thus, one slowly spreads the ten fingers of both hands.
Once this rite has been performed, all devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans shall see the practitioner as a vajra-body clad in vajra-mail.
All Māras, heterodox spirits, and the like dare not look upon him directly; they retreat and flee, unable to cause harm.
Having performed this rite, he next visualizes the image of the primary deity before him. He contemplates his own form as that of Avalokiteśvara as usual.
Furthermore, as previously described, within the five-jeweled chamber of Mount Sumeru, he single-mindedly and attentively contemplates Amitābha in its midst.
The Buddha’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs radiate with blazing light.
To the Buddha’s right stands the holy being Avalokiteśvara; to the Buddha’s left is the Bodhisattva Vimalacārin.
Slightly to the right of the Buddha’s front is the holy Tārāmaitrī Tathāgata, arising from the syllable *hrīḥ*, appearing in the form of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Formless Stainless (Vimalarūpa) arises from the syllable *sa*; the Holy Tārā arises from the syllable *ba*;
the Bodhisattva Tārā arises from the syllable *praṇa*. To the right is a messenger named Ekajaṭī;
this holy one arises from the transformation of the syllable *e*. To the right of the Bodhisattva Vimalacaryā is a *vidyādhara*.
There are koṭis of bodhisattvas; these bodhisattvas arise from the syllable *vi*. To the left, there is a Hayagrīva Bodhisattva;
this bodhisattva arises from which syllable? Their forms and such characteristics are as extensively described in the sūtra.
Before the Buddha, there is a Pṛthivīdevatā; this deity arises from the syllable *pa*. As for her form...
One should visualize deities stationed at each of the four directions as their guardians. The deity in the east is named Indra;
this deity’s female form wears adamantine armor and holds an adamantine vajra, protecting the eastern direction.
In the south is a deity named Yama; this deity’s female form wears only a simple robe and armor and holds the staff of Yama, protecting the southern direction.
In the western direction, there is a deity named Pāruṇī who is clad in armor, assumes a female form, and wields a bow and arrows while guarding the west.
In the northern direction, there is a deity named Kuberi whose appearance and armor are exactly as described before;
she holds a flower-topped staff in her hand and guards the north. All such deities possess majestic radiance.
One must cause the visualization to be vivid, as if facing it directly before one's eyes.
Having performed this contemplation of the dharma, one again visualizes the syllables of the root mantra within the body: first, visualize the syllable *Oṃ* at the crown of the head;
next, visualize the syllable *Ta* on the forehead; then, visualize the syllable *Li* on the two eyes; and finally, visualize the syllable *Ttha* placed upon the throat.
Furthermore, one should visualize the syllable *ma* upon the two shoulders; again, visualize the syllable *re* upon the heart; then, visualize the syllable *du* upon the navel;
next, visualize the syllable *ri* upon the two calves of the thighs; then, visualize the syllable *svā* upon the two shins;
and finally, visualize the syllable *hā* upon the tops of the two feet. One should now contemplate these ten syllables as being distributed throughout the body.
Having already performed this, one again forms the seal of the precious chariot (*ratnasyandana-mudrā*) to welcome the various holy ones and others.

For this reason, one first performs the visualization of the original body of the deity, and only thereafter invites the holy ones. Having visualized each of the deities and understood their characteristics, one then invites the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) to approach the dharma-substance.
For this purpose, when first visualizing and inviting [the deities], one should employ the seal of the precious chariot.
With both hands palms facing upward, interlace the three fingers from the index finger downward toward the inside;
support the sides of the two index fingers against each other and push the tips of the middle fingers inward with the thumbs. This is called the *ratnayaṣṭi-mudrā* (Jewel-Staff Seal).

Visualize this as a jewel chariot and proceed to the abodes of the various Honored Ones (*bhadra*). Visualize that all the Honored Ones together mount this jewel chariot and arrive; contemplate them within this chariot.
One visualizes above there is a jeweled chamber, adorned with various treasures and covered by a net of jewels from which bells and pendants hang all around;
within the spaces of the net are exquisite maṇi-jewels, their subtle light shining brightly as one ascends upon clouds of five colors to fly upward.
The seal-mantra for this is as follows:

Oṃ (1) tulu tulu (2) hūṃ. Having recited this mantra, one should first visualize the deity at the site using the aforementioned mudrā. Then, with the heart-mantra and mudrā of one’s own family, one invites the Noble One to descend.
As for the heart-mudrā of the family: interlace the ten fingers of both hands inwardly to form fists, then draw them apart.
Stepping out to the right, the Great Mother pointed inward and beckoned him with this mantra: *Oṃ āruḷi svāhā*.
First, she went forward to welcome him with the Jewel-Cart Seal and mantra; next, she further invited him to descend with the Family Heart-mantra and seal.
When those who have come together for the practitioner’s sake receive offerings and benefit humans and devas, they arrive;

at that time, one should summon them using the seal and mantra of Hayagrīva Bodhisattva. As for the seal: with both hands, interlace the three fingers from the index finger downward outward to form fists;
cross the two thumbs, placing the right over the left; then bend the backs of the middle joints of the two index fingers.
The mantra for the mutual binding is as follows:
Oṃ (1) hāye jili-bha (2) mahā-padma (3) kuśa-karṣaya (4) śigalaṃ (5) sarva-padma-kūla (6) samudra-padma.
(7) *Kuśadala* (8) *Huṃja*. (Recite this seal-mantra with an entering tone; it appears in the *Ghaṇṭākarṇa Sūtra*). One should use this seal-mantra to summon [the chariot].
When summoning, beckon it with the index finger. Once the chariot has arrived, again use the original seal-mantra to cause it to descend.
Grasp its right wrist with the left hand and place the left hand upon the crown of the head, facing [it].
The mantra for summoning from afar is:
Oṃ (1) sarvasattvānām (2) āhe āhe (3) svāhā. Using this seal and mantra, one descends the precious chariot;
having descended the precious chariot, when entering the precious chamber, one again uses this seal.
To cause the mantra to enter, join the two hands with the palms hollowed and the fingertips touching;
then interlace the two index fingers, placing the right over the left. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) amoghadharma-paśya (2) krodha (3) ākarṣaya (4) praveśaya (5) mahāpraśvāsita (6) yama-paruṇa (7) kubera-brahma (8) oṃ vaiśadara (9) padmaku-ra (10) sa (3)
MAYAN (11) HŪṂ HŪṂ (12). With this seal and mantra, invite all the mantra-devas and others from within the lotus to enter the precious chamber.

Once they have entered, further arrange seats for them to sit upon. The seal for sitting is formed by joining the wrists of both hands and extending the ten fingers straight upward, slightly fanned apart.
Visualizing it as being like an opening lotus, the mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) sarva-prativiṣṭha (2) bodhanāya (3) svāhā.
Having established the seats with this mantra-seal and invited the deities to sit, one should immediately offer them scented water; this is the water.
It is called the Akā-water seal. To form the seal: with the two hands, clench the thumbs by grasping the three fingers from the index finger downward into fists;
then bend the tips of the two index fingers so they touch each other. The mantra is as follows: [Mantra]
Oṃ (1) sarva-utkaca-garjāya (2) svāhā. With this mantra, one should offer water from the seal-mudrā, having mixed it with white sandalwood paste and the like.
Having made the water offering, one should immediately perform the door-closing mudrā by joining the two hands in the hollowed *añjali* gesture and then bending the two index fingers upward.
Cross the left hand over the right, pressing the two thumbs against each other with the right thumb over the left;
grasp the tips of the index fingers and recite the mantra: Oṃ (1) padma (2) saṃbhūta-paṇḍita (3) sarva-padma-kula (4).
Samaya (5), Jālaṃ (6), Hūṃ (7). Reciting this mantra and employing this mudrā, one should seal the four gates of the precious chamber before oneself.
Having performed this rite, one further performs the mudrā and mantra of Joy, causing all the noble ones to be greatly delighted: join the two hands together with their two tips...
Bend the fingers so that their tips touch one another, place the thumbs side-by-side and bend them into the palms, and recite the mantra:
Oṃ (1) samukha-van-kumāra (2) vaiśadara (3) padmakaṇṭhāya viśaya (4) sarva-padma-kula (5) samudra (6) sarva.
Mūlaṃ (7) paṇḍaye (8) sarvasiddhiyomi (9) prāyeche (10) padmavaiśe (11) ā ā ā ā (12).
Having performed this rite, one then purifies the ground and binds the lower direction with the vajra-muṣṭi mudrā, pressing the left middle finger down.
With the right hands crossed, place the tips against each other; the two ring fingers are likewise pressed left over right.

With the crossed hands, place the tips against the space between the little fingers, with the tips of the two little fingers supporting one another, and the tips of the index fingers likewise supporting each other.
Join the tips of the two thumbs together and touch them. The mantra says:
Oṃ (1) kili kili (2) vajrapūra (3) bandha bandha (4) hūṃ (5) phaṭ (6) svāhā.
By touching the earth with this mudrā, one can cause all vināyakas of the lower direction to depart entirely.
Having performed this rite, one further forms the seal for binding and protecting the four directions.
This seal follows the previous procedure, with the only modification being that the two thumbs are held upright. The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) sara sara (2) vajra (3) prākāra (4) hūṃ (5) phaṭ (6)

Recite the mantra "Svāhā" while circling this mudrā three times around the body; this immediately establishes the boundary of the four directions. This rite removes the demonic obstacles of the four directions.
Having performed this rite, one should then bind the boundary of the upper direction; the mudrā follows the previous form, with the only modification being that the two heads are changed.
Interlace the fingers so that the tips of the two thumbs and the tips of the two index fingers touch one another,
and recite the mantra: Oṃ (1) viśpu-ra (2) narakṣa (3) vajrapañjara (4) hūṃ (5) phaṭ (6) svāhā.
Having bound the boundary above with this seal-mantra and completed this protective rite for the Dharma, one should first perform the four kinds of secret inner and outer offerings.
Regarding the first of these, the four inner seals: the first is named *pātrama-lakṣa*.
To form its mudrā, join the two hands in the usual *añjali* gesture, with the four fingers below the index fingers held together as usual.
Then, opening the middle [fingers] and again extending the two thumbs toward the body,
recite the mantra: Oṃ (1) Dharmarājīkaraṇa (2) Mahārathikara (3) Pūjāsamaye (4) Hūṃ.
The second is the mudrā of Bodhināgama-ra (Mālā). Following the previous mudrā, extend the fingers forward;
the mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) dharmamātṛ (2) viśodhaya (3) āvileka (4) puṣya-saṃ (3).

MĀYE HŪṂ. This third is called the *Dharmagītā* (Chanting) mudrā. Following the previous mudrā, again draw [the hands] together at the heart, then slowly open them upward and spread the fingers; the mantra is as follows:

Oṃ (1) dharmagīte (2) avatārita (3) puṣyasamaye (4) hūṃ. This fourth [mudrā] is named the Dharmadharakṣitendra (Dance) Mudrā. To perform this mudrā, follow the previous method: place it at the heart, then rotate the right hand over the left hand and slowly raise it to the head.

The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) dharmagīte (2) avatārita (3) puṣyasamaye (4) hūṃ. This fourth [mudrā] is named the Dharmadharakṣitendra (Dance) Mudrā. To perform this mudrā, follow the previous method:
place it at the heart, then rotate the right hand over the left hand and slowly raise it to the head. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) dharmākarṣaya (2) sarvabhuja (3) parivartana (4) samaya (5) hūṃ.
The above is called the method for the four types of offerings of the inner court. Regarding the four external [offerings], the first is incense.
Form the seal by joining the ten fingers of both hands, crossing them with the right over the left, and then slowly opening the hands downward.
The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) padma-dūpa (2) puṣpa-samaye (3) praharaṇāya.
(4) *Bhadrakurande* (5) *Mahāgani* (6) *Padmarati* (7) *Hūṃ*. Regarding the second flower mudrā:
having joined the two hands in the usual manner of palms-joined (*añjali*), one immediately opens them and spreads them upward.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) puṣpapūjāsamaye (2) dharmamālini (3) mahāśriye (4) dharmakūṭa (5) pratihari (6) sarvārtha.
(7) SṬAD-YA (6) HŪM. Regarding the mudrā of the third lamp:
interlace the two hands with the right over the left, turning them outward to form fists, and place both thumbs side by side pressing down upon the tops of the fists. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) dīpa-pūja-samaye (2) dharma-sundari (3) mahānuttaye (4) loka-sañjñāye (5) dharma-sarasvati (6) hūṃ. Fourth, the Incense Mudrā:
As for the form of this mudrā, join the palms as usual, then open the wrists within the hollow of the hands.
Pointing the hand toward the heart and dispersing it,
the mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) khaṇḍarohasamaye (2) mahādharmakūṭaciti (3) kuru sarvakarmāṇi me (4) dharmasiddhi (5) hūṃ.
Next, the method for the mudrā and mantra of offering food shall be explained:
one should place both hands flat, palms upward, with the sides touching each other. The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) sarvatathāgata (2) rasarasā (3) yūrodrabhuja-samaye (4) hūṃ.
The above mudrās are called the Mudrās and Mantras for the Offering of Food and Drink.
Next, the method for the bodily offering of the Seal Division (*mudrā-bhaga*) and the Repentance Seal (*pratideśanā-mudrā*) will be explained:
Having joined the two hands in the usual *añjali* gesture, bend the two little fingers so that their backs touch and the tips of the two index fingers meet. The mantra is as follows:
Tadyathā (1) aridatari (2) dhatari (3) dhuri (4) helanayage ravai (5) rakṣa rakṣa maṃ (6) sarvanokṣivye (7) sarvopadravivye (8) svāhā.
This is called the Root Seal. One who repents before the Buddha while forming this seal can extinguish immeasurable grave offenses.
Furthermore, one forms the Mind Seal by changing only the two thumbs to grasp the index fingers and placing them at the heart. The mantra is: [Mantra]
Oṃ (1) sarva-hṛdaya (3) sambuddhāya (4) svāhā.
When making this offering, one is able to eliminate the sins of the three karmas of the practitioner.
Next, the method for the oral mudrā is explained according to the preceding heart mudrā, with this sole modification:
bend both thumbs into the palms and press them against the upper parts of the little fingers. The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) vimalaśi (2) gagana (3) svāhā.
The power of this seal and mantra can eliminate all verbal transgressions of the practitioner.
Next, the seal for removing all obscurations (*sarvāvaraṇaviṣkambhin*) is taught: press the tip of the middle finger with the thumb of the right hand, and do the same with the left;
then join the right hand over the left hand and recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ (1) sarvabuddhabodhisattvāya (2) svāhā. Next, the mudrā for summoning all devas and nāgas is taught:
having covered with the left hand and extended the five fingers long, one then forms a fist with the right hand pointing downward;
with the index finger of the left hand pointing forward, one summons [them] while reciting the mantra.
Oṃ (1) kuluṭa (2) babadhibabānāṃ (3) svāhā. Reciting this mantra is used to summon the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.
Next, the mudrā for binding and protecting all directions and realms to expel obstacles is explained: First, interlace the two ring fingers with the left pressing over the right;
then, press the right middle finger over the left ring finger; next, press the tip of the left thumb against the head of the right little finger;
finally, grasp the right middle finger with the tips of the left middle finger, index finger, and ring finger.
Form a fist by pressing the right thumb against the back of the left middle finger and so forth; then, join the tips of the right index finger with the tip of the left little finger.
Rotate this seal around the body, brandishing it at a distance determined by the practitioner’s intention for protection;
in all such cases, success shall be achieved. The mantra is as follows: [Mantra]
Oṃ (1) sarvayakṣarākṣasa (2) bandha bandha (3) svāhā. Next, perform the mudrā for purifying the five eyes:
join the two hands in the hollowed *añjali* gesture, then bend the tips of the two index fingers so they touch each other, and press them with the thumbs.
Next, place the two ring fingers against the nails of the little fingers. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ (1) sarvacakṣu-karaṇāya (3) svāhā. By forming this mudrā, the five eyes shall always be purified.
Next, perform the Varada-mudrā (the Gesture of Granting Boons): with the left hand, press the tip of the index finger with the thumb and extend the remaining three fingers;

do the same with the right hand. Hold the left hand upright and let the right hang down. While using the aforementioned mantra to form this mudrā, one can cause all sentient beings of the six realms to be free from all suffering and affliction.
Next, perform the mudrā for summoning the Four Kings: with the three fingers from the middle finger downward of both hands, cross the right over the left toward the inside;
bend the two thumbs within the palms and hook the two index fingers inward. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) sarvadevākarṣaya (2) svāhā. By forming this mudrā, one summons the Four Heavenly Kings and may inquire about the affairs of the four continents as one desires.

Next, perform the *bandha-mudrā* (binding seal): interlace the ten fingers of both hands with the palms facing inward, then extend and erect the two index fingers so that their tips touch one another;
do the same for the two little fingers. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) sarvadeva-utka svāhā. When forming this mudrā, one can subjugate Varuṇa. Next, form the fire-restraining mudrā:
on top of the water mudrā, simply change the tips of the index and little fingers so that they are slightly separated.
The mantra is recited as follows:
Oṃ (1) Aghnaye (2) Sarvabhūtānām (3) Aghnaye (4) Svāhā. Next, perform the mudrā for subduing wind-disasters:
first, interlace the middle and ring fingers of the right hand with those of the left.
On the back of the ring finger, insert the index and little fingers to press upon the ring finger and middle finger of the left hand at the heart;
with the index and little fingers of the left hand, press the middle and ring fingers of the right hand from above.
Extend the two thumbs, keeping them straight and vertical, turn the palms outward, and form this *vāyu-mudrā* (wind seal) to sustain all winds.
None of these difficulties shall cause harm. All the Wind and Rain Deity Kings shall submit and follow [the command].
The mantra for the Wind Seal is: Oṃ (1) Maya-vai (2) Sarva-ma-kulu-ta (3) Nivata-ya (4) Svāhā.
Next, perform the Pure Precept Seal: having placed the right knee upon the ground, join the palms as usual and leave them hollow.
In the middle [of the hands], place each of the two index fingers upon the back of the two middle fingers, and place each of the two thumbs beneath the two index fingers.
The mantra is as follows: Oṃ (1) sarvaprati- (2) mukha-kṣa-hṛdaye (3) svāhā.
When forming this mudrā, it enables all infinite sentient beings to attain the body of pure precepts.
Next, perform the mudrā for subduing thieves: with the index, middle, ring, and little fingers of both hands, hook them together;
extend the four fingers of the left hand and hold the two thumbs apart and upright. When forming this mudrā, all dangers from thieves [are averted].
All are completely bound and unable to cause harm.
The mantra says: Oṃ (1) sarvatucchata (2) pratuschatānām (3) chindaya (4) svāhā.
The Seal of Intelligence (*Prājñā-mudrā*): With the two thumbs, pinch the upper joints of the two ring fingers respectively.

The two little fingers are held straight up and pressed against each other. The sides of the two middle fingers are bent inward to touch, and the tips of the two index fingers are placed against the second joints of the two middle fingers, about one inch apart.
Forming this seal at the center of the chest, if there is [an object] before one...
For those of dull faculties, this seal-offering shall fulfill their aspirations. Within the kingdom of King Phalirāja, there was a great and wealthy householder who was by nature of dull faculties;
yet by making a vow for seven days, he immediately attained sharp faculties and could recite a thousand verses daily.
Other proofs of its efficacy cannot be detailed here. One should recite the aforementioned root mantra.
The Seal for Opening the Gates of Hell: With the two middle fingers and ring fingers, each bent into the palm with their backs facing one another;

the two thumbs, index fingers, and little fingers each separated by about half an inch—when this seal is formed, the gates of hell open and the sentient beings suffering therein are simultaneously liberated; King Yama rejoices and praises it, beholding [this].
Out of great compassion and pity for all living beings, [the Buddha] preached this essential Dharma to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
One should also recite the root mantra and form the seal for rebirth in the pure lands of the ten directions: with palms joined at the heart, place both thumbs side by side against the chest.
When forming this seal, one should recite the mantra with single-minded devotion for the sake of all sentient beings as they approach the end of life, performing the ritual of the seal.
If one wishes to be born in a particular Buddha-land, one may be reborn there at will by reciting the root mantra.
To visualize the seal of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: interlace the two ring fingers and little fingers with the right hand over the left;
join the tips of the two middle fingers together and hold them upright; and bend the second joints of the two index fingers.
Furthermore, at the third stage, with the two thumbs turned away from each other, press the joints of the two index fingers;
while maintaining focused and correct mindfulness, when the manifestation appears, having seen it, one should repent. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will speak to the practitioner, saying:
"What wish do you desire? Your wishes shall all be fulfilled. One who performs this rite should recite the root mantra.
The Seal of Universal Gathering: With both wrists crossed with palms facing upward, press the right thumb over the left thumb;
clench both hands into tight fists while holding the eight fingers. This seal universally gathers all mother-dhāraṇīs. The mantra for the Seal of Universal Gathering is as follows: [Mantra]
Oṃ (1) sarvanayuta (2) mudrāya (3) bandha bandha (4) svāhā. This is the seal of the fulfillment of the six perfections.
Join the backs of both hands together with palms facing inward; turn the wrists outward and place the two thumbs at the mid-brow, pointing downward.
While forming this seal, arouse the bodhicitta and contemplate all sentient beings.

Their birth is like that of infants; all sentient beings are fully endowed with the six pāramitās, their aspirations are fulfilled, and all Buddhas throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges rejoice. The mantra says:
Tadyathā (1) sarvabuddhāya (2) sarvapariśram (3) pāramitāyai (4) oṃ (5) hohavasa (6) svāhā (7). Tadyathā (8) mridatari (9) svāhā.
The Seal of the Divine Power (*ṛddhipāda-mudrā*): First, bend the middle and ring fingers of the right hand into the palm and press the thumb against the middle phalanges of the ring fingers.
While reciting the root mantra, rub both feet; one will travel a thousand *li* in a single day.

When performing this seal, the Earth Goddess (*pṛthivī-devatā*) will support the feet of the practitioner with a pedestal of seven precious jewels. Those of ordinary fleshly eyes cannot [perceive this].

If one sees [the deity] and gives rise only to a heart of compassion and a mind to rescue and protect, without seeking fame or gain, one will surely receive the assistance of the ten thousand deities.
To perform the seal according to the mind: extend the index finger of the right hand and the little finger of the left hand, leaving a space of about one inch between them.
When forming this seal while reciting the root mantra, all one's aspirations shall be fulfilled.
This is the Seal for Subduing All Devas and Nāgas: With the right hand, press down upon the backs of the four fingers of the left hand, interlacing them with the tips pointing downward;
then, moving the four fingers of the left hand back and forth, recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ (1) kuruṭa (2) sarvadevatā (3) svāhā. This is the mudrā for entering the six realms while remaining invisible:
With the right hand, press the thumb upon the tip of the middle fingernail of the ring finger;
extend the index and little fingers straight upward. The left hand is likewise positioned, with the thumb inserted from below and moving upward.
With the right palm, hook the middle and ring fingers of the left hand, and press the right fingers over the left fingers.
The mantra is: Oṃ (1) kūjaye ti (2) sarvakāliyanī (3) svāhā. When performing this mudrā, one travels freely with a hidden form;
all that one sets one's heart upon shall be fulfilled according to one's wishes.

The Body Seal of Bodhisattva Tāre: Interlace the three fingers from the middle finger downward with their palms facing inward, join the two index fingers together and hold them upright, and extend the two thumbs side by side. The mantra is as follows: [mantra].
Oṃ (1) tārī tārī (2) dhūtārī (3) dhūtārī (4) dhurī dhurī (5) svāhā. When performing any of these mudrās, one must maintain strict secrecy;
they must not be performed in impure places or in the open air.
One should not form the mudrās with a casual mind; when binding the mudrās, one should cover them with a clean cloth so that others do not see them.
Furthermore, those who have not yet entered the *samādhi* maṇḍala must not stand before one while binding the mudrās.
Only after making this offering of mudrās should one settle the mind and perform the recitation. During the recitation, one should chant this mantra.
Oṃ (1) Tāri (2) Tutāri (3) Turi (4) Svāhā. If one recites this mantra, or recites it together with the preceding root mantra,
one shall behold each of these mantra-syllables emerging from the mouth of the primary deity,
emitting light of the seven precious gems that enters the practitioner’s mouth, passes through the heart, and revolves upon the moon disc within.
Having performed the visualization of the rosary, one should then recite the mantra using lotus-seed beads (*padmākṣa*).
When counting the beads, one should hold them with the thumb and the ring finger pressed together.
At the beginning of the recitation, one should grasp the beads and recite the *sūkṣma-hṛdaya-mantra* three times. The mantra is as follows: [Mantra omitted]
Oṃ (1) kuru kule (2) svāhā. Reciting this dharma-mantra, one should do so as much as desired according to one's inclination;
one should extensively make great vows and petition for whatever one intends to accomplish.
Whether one can or not, one should form all the seals previously mentioned, or at least the [śa-ku] seal. If one is unable to form them all, [one should form the primary seal].
As for the binding, one may simply bind the three previously mentioned samaya-mudrās;
having bound this mudrā as well, one should recite this mantra to dispatch the deities. The mantra is: Oṃ kṛtvo paśya sarvasattvārthasiddhidadhe tvaṃ nuga.
Kechara (2), Dṛśabhadra-viṣaya (3), Punarāga (4), Manaye dūṃ vajra-dharma.
Reciting this mantra, join the lotus-samādhi mudrā;
raise the mudrā and place it upon the head, then release it as it was originally.
The ritual for the Dharma is likewise identical. Having again made vows and performed the dedication of merit as before, one prostrates to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others.
Scattering [the offerings], one contemplates oneself as a Bodhisattva and returns to one's original form.
Constantly giving rise to a mind of rescue and deliverance toward all sentient beings, one may thereafter leave the essential chamber at will.
*The Dharma of the Bodhisattva Padmottara-citta*, one fascicle.

On the night of the second watch on the third day of the middle winter in the year of Renyin, the second year of the Tenmei era, this was transcribed from the copy held in the Ryūunzō collection and collated.
As for that original manuscript, it was [copied] at Nanzan during the Hōei era.
Gyōkō of the Potalaka-in transcribed this based on an ancient manuscript from Nyoirin-ji and further collated and punctuated it using another version.
On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month of that same year, [he completed this] based on the *Tattvārtha-svacitta-dhāraṇī* translated by Jitong.
Having completed the collation against the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
this transcription was finished on the fifth day of the tenth month in the year of Jīmūta (the sixth year of Kōan),
the fifty-third year of Prince Yūō of the Eastern Capital. (Age fifty-three.)
